text: Processors are required to implement cGMP controls that prevent allergen cross‑contact, including controls that are part of the prerequisite program and/or sanitation monitoring procedures to prevent cross‑contact in areas such as incoming ingredients, processing, storage, and handling. These controls provide separation in time and space between products with different allergenic ingredients and are tailored to the facility and product. [fda_seafood_ch19:2:0]

The final regulation permitting the use of ionizing radiation on raw meat and meat products was issued by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food Safety and Inspection Service (USDA/FSIS). [fda_food_code_2026:424:0]

Written environmental monitoring procedures should be scientifically valid and include: specifying whether testing is for Listeria spp. or L. monocytogenes; identifying the locations and number of sampling sites; determining the timing and frequency of sample collection and testing; specifying the test(s) and analytical method(s) used; naming the laboratory performing the testing; and incorporating corrective action procedures to be followed when Listeria spp. or L. monocytogenes is detected. [fda_lm_rte_2017:41:0]
Shell eggs packed for consumer use must be stored and transported at an ambient temperature not to exceed 7.2 °C (45 °F). [fda_food_code_2026:431:0]
The two primary ways to reduce water activity in foods are (1) product formulation, such as adding salt or sugar, and (2) dehydration (drying). [fda_pchf_ch04:24:0]

The process log for each production line should include the plant or facility identification, dates (and when appropriate, times) of monitoring, the signature or initials of the person performing the monitoring (e.g., operator initials), and evidence of review (i.e., the initials of the PCQI or designee). [fda_pchf_ch06:15:0]

No. A foreign facility that exported food to the United States and later determines that the food is reportable is not required to submit a reportable food report for recipients outside the United States; FDA may require information only about U.S. recipients. [fda_rfr_qa_ed2:30:0]

The FDA recommends that a seafood processor develop a written sanitation program that includes procedures, practices, and processes to keep the facility in a condition that significantly minimizes allergen cross‑contact. The program should identify what is to be cleaned, define a cleaning frequency that reflects processing schedules, equipment type, products, and allergen risk, and provide detailed instructions on equipment breakdown, chemicals, concentrations, temperature set‑points, and other critical factors for effective cleaning. It should also include monitoring and verification steps to ensure that food‑contact surfaces, utensils, staff wardrobe, and equipment are effectively cleaned and sanitized. [fda_seafood_app10:1:2]

The regulation of pesticides in food is shared by three federal agencies: the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and the U.S. Department of Agriculture Food Safety and Inspection Service (USDA FSIS). [fda_pchf_ch03:22:1]

Physical hazards are broadly classified as “hard/sharp” physical hazards and “choking” hazards. These categories can cause injuries such as dental damage, laceration of the mouth or throat, laceration or perforation of the intestine, choking, and even death. [fda_pchf_ch03:33:1]

An establishment must identify all possible post‑lethality food‑contact surfaces (FCSs) for sampling, the sample size for each FCS, the sampling frequency (e.g., number of samples per month per line), the total number of samples to collect routinely, and provide a justification that the sampling frequency is sufficient to maintain effective control of Lm or Listeria spp. [fsis_dir_10240_4_r4:13:1]

Cookie Processor B’s corrective action procedures for a low oven temperature specify that the cookies will be diverted to further processing (such as baking for cookie‑crumbs ingredient production) or to animal food (non‑pet food); maintenance will determine the cause of the low temperature and fix the oven so the temperature is reset to the operating limit of 352 °F (178 °C) before more cookies are baked; and employees will be retrained, if necessary, on the importance of ensuring that the oven temperature has reached the set point before allowing the line to run. [fda_pchf_ch06:24:1]

The Salmonidae family includes pink salmon, coho salmon, sockeye salmon, chinook salmon, Atlantic salmon, chum salmon, rainbow trout, cutthroat trout, and brown trout, all of which may be fed with canthaxanthin or astaxanthin color additives. [fda_food_code_2026:497:0]

Receiving facilities under subpart G of part 117 are establishments that manufacture or process a raw material or other ingredient that they receive from a supplier. Examples include a facility that manufactures or processes produce raw agricultural commodities (RACs) into bagged salads, a facility that mills grains such as wheat to make flour, and a facility that manufactures cookies using flour, sugar and other ingredients. [fda_pchf_ch15:5:1]

Good hygiene practices alone may not be sufficient when the food operation is complex, involves specific hazards that GHPs do not control, or when technological advances or special end‑use requirements create additional risks. In such cases, significant hazards identified through a hazard analysis that are not controlled by GHPs must be addressed in a HACCP plan. [codex_cxc1_1969:8:0]

Melamine is considered a significant chemical hazard that must be addressed in a food safety plan when the ingredient (e.g., milk products) comes from a country where melamine adulteration has occurred or when there is a documented history of melamine being added for economic gain. In such cases, the hazard analysis should include the potential for melamine as an economically‑motivated adulterant and require preventive controls. If no history of melamine adulteration exists for the country of origin, it is not regarded as a significant hazard. [fda_pchf_ch03:27:0, fda_pchf_ch03:26:0]

Waste must be stored in covered containers and kept in a location that does not contaminate food, storage areas or the environment, and it must be removed at regular intervals, at least daily, to prevent buildup and pest access. The waste storage area and any receptacles or equipment that have come into contact with waste must be cleaned and disinfected immediately after disposal, and the storage area should be cleaned and disinfected at least daily. The disposal of sewage and effluents must comply with environmental regulations, and drainage and waste‑disposal systems must be designed so that food or potable water is not contaminated. [fssai_sched4_compendium:45:1, fssai_sched4_compendium:45:3, fssai_sched4_compendium:45:4, fssai_sched4_compendium:45:5, fssai_sched4_compendium:82:1]
The recommended volume of primary enrichment transferred from each sponge or swab into the secondary enrichment broth when compositing up to five samples is 0.1 ± 0.02 mL. [fda_lm_rte_2017:84:0]

The RO is responsible for coordinating effectiveness checks and directing FSIS personnel activities. It must determine product distribution, request assistance from Assisting Offices, and decide whether additional consignees should be added to the distribution list. The RO eliminates duplicate consignee listings, uploads the list into APM, and assigns the appropriate number of on‑site and telephone checks using the tables in Attachment 1. It may group checks by special consignee categories and apply the relevant table to each category. Finally, the RO selects a subset of consignees for checks using the selection criteria in Attachment 1. [fsis_dir_8080_1_r8:15:0]

To regain control after a critical limit deviation involving mislabeled allergen information, the operation should either discontinue use of the supplier or work with the supplier to ensure corrections are made to prevent recurrence. [fda_seafood_ch19:11:2]

If maintenance employees cannot be excluded from RTE areas during operations, they should change outer clothing and any other soiled clothing, use separate tools for raw and RTE areas (or wash and sanitize tools and hands prior to entering RTE areas), and wear only freshly cleaned/sanitized footwear in such areas. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:75:0]
Food employees must vigorously rub the surfaces of their lathered hands and arms for at least 20 seconds, then rinse thoroughly with clean water. [fsis_sps_guide:75:0]
If a consignee is unsure whether they handled the recalled product, they should follow the recall instructions and conduct a sub‑recall. [fda_iom2026_ch07:17:0]

No. A positive test for Listeria spp. on a food contact surface does not automatically make the product adulterated; the product is only considered adulterated if the surface tests positive for Listeria monocytogenes (Lm)【fsis_lm_rte_2014:127:0】【fsis_lm_rte_2014:85:1】

If meat and poultry products are cooled slowly after partial cooking that does not reach full lethality, the spores of Clostridia can survive the heat treatment and then multiply during the cooling period, potentially reaching excessive growth levels that pose a food‑safety risk. [fsis_appendix_b_2021:12:0]

Incorporating HACCP principles into routine inspections gives operators constructive input needed to establish a control system that keeps foodborne‑illness risk factors under continuous control, fostering continuous problem‑solving and prevention. [fda_food_code_2026:593:0]

Recipe management is a process control that ensures food ingredients are added within their maximum use levels, preventing misformulation and chemical hazards. It involves using recipe cards or similar documentation to specify ingredient amounts and critical limits, and monitoring and verifying these steps during production. This control is part of an active managerial approach to food safety, supported by SOPs, monitoring procedures, and record‑keeping. [fda_pchf_ch04:29:0]

The FDA guidance identifies intrinsic characteristics that can prevent the growth of *Listeria monocytogenes* in ready‑to‑eat foods, including: a pH ≤ 4.4; a water activity ≤ 0.92; and the presence of one or more inhibitory substances (e.g., sorbic acid, benzoic acid, or naturally occurring antimicrobials from fermentation) that, alone or in combination, act as listeristatic hurdles. These characteristics can be naturally present or deliberately introduced during processing. [fda_lm_rte_2017:32:0] [fda_lm_rte_2017:3:0] [fda_lm_rte_2017:10:0]

Corrective action for a sulfiting deviation is to reject the affected lot and discontinue use of the supplier until evidence is obtained that control of sulfiting agent content has improved. [fda_seafood_ch19:13:2, fda_seafood_ch19:15:2]

Yes, an establishment that moves to a new physical location will most likely need to repeat the in‑plant validation element of its initial HACCP validation because the new location may have different operational parameters that affect the execution of the control measures. This reassessment is required to gather new in‑plant data that support the second element of validation. The scientific support can be transferred, but in‑plant data must be collected at the new site to demonstrate that the critical operational parameters are being met. [fsis_haccp_validation:32:0]
Not found in the provided documents.

The process approach to HACCP is a method of hazard analysis that divides the many food flows in a retail or food‑service establishment into broad categories based on activities or stages in the preparation of the food, then analyzes the hazards and places managerial controls on each grouping. This approach uses the food preparation processes common to a specific operation rather than individual food commodities, making it more efficient and useful for operators who handle many different foods simultaneously. [fda_food_code_2026:585:0] [fda_retail_haccp_manual:17:0]
Intensified sampling is initiated after a second positive Food Contact Surface (FCS) result. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:117:0]
Soup Processor A’s PCQI reviews corrective‑action records as part of a pre‑shipment review before a lot of soup is released, ensuring all lot records are in order. [fda_pchf_ch06:29:1]
Cleaning‑chemical containers must be kept in clearly identified, separate storage away from food materials to prevent contamination. [fssai_sched4_compendium:44:2, fssai_sched4_compendium:51:0]

Irradiation of food in the United States uses ionizing radiation from two approved sources: gamma rays emitted by radioactive cobalt‑60 or cesium‑137, and X‑rays produced by high‑energy electron accelerators that strike a heavy‑metal target. [fda_pchf_ch04:13:2]

Cabinets used for storing food, cleaned and sanitized equipment, utensils, laundered linens, or single‑service/single‑use articles may not be located in locker rooms, toilet rooms, garbage rooms, mechanical rooms, under unshielded sewer lines, under leaking or condensed water lines, under open stairwells, or under other sources of contamination. Cabinets for linens or single‑service/single‑use articles may be stored in a locker room. [fda_food_code_2026:129:0]

A facility can be considered compliant with 9 CFR 416.2(d) when condensation is present on a drip pan but has been reduced through fan installation, provided that the establishment has taken reasonable measures to minimize the condensation and maintains the surface in a clean and sanitary condition so that the condensation cannot adulterate product. This is illustrated in the example where the drip pan’s bottom surface is kept sanitary and the condensation evaporates quickly, meeting the regulation’s requirement that condensation be controlled to prevent adulteration. The guidance in the Sanitation Performance Standards Compliance Guide confirms that condensation expected from certain operations must be documented and controlled—typically by cleaning and sanitizing the surfaces where it forms—to avoid creating insanitary conditions or product adulteration. Thus, the facility’s actions of installing fans and cleaning the drip pan align with the regulation’s intent to control condensation and protect product safety. [fsis_dir_5000_1_r8:13:0] [fsis_sps_guide:18:0]

Sanitation controls must include procedures, practices, and processes that prevent allergen cross‑contact and cross‑contamination from insanitary objects and from personnel to food, food‑packaging material, other food‑contact surfaces, and from raw product to processed product. These controls are required to cover the prevention of allergen cross‑contact. [fda_pchf_ch04:35:0]

A slaughter establishment that is not very low volume must sample cattle, sheep, goats, horses, mules or other equines at a rate of **one test per 300 carcasses, but at a minimum of one sample during each week of operation**. [fsis_dir_5000_1_r8:48:0]  

Very low‑volume establishments that collect samples by sponging must collect **at least one sample per week** (starting the first full week of operation after June 1 each year and continuing until 13 samples have been collected or until June 1 of the following year). [fsis_dir_5000_1_r8:48:0]

A HACCP plan is not required for a TCS food packaged using reduced‑oxygen packaging in a food establishment when the food is (1) labeled with the production time and date, (2) held at 5 °C (41 °F) or less during refrigerated storage, and (3) removed from its package in the food establishment within 48 hours after packaging. [fda_food_code_2026:107:1, fda_food_code_2026:697:0]

A food product must be **safe and wholesome**—meaning it contains no ingredients that pose a public‑health concern and is free from contamination such as Listeria monocytogenes—so that it can be donated under USDA FSIS guidelines. It must also be **economically adulterated only in a manner that does not mislead consumers**; that is, any omitted, substituted, or removed valuable ingredients must not create a false impression of the food’s identity, composition, or quality, and any labeling must be accurate or properly approved. The product must have a “Not for Sale” statement on each immediate container if it contains incorrectly labeled ingredients of public‑health concern, and it must obtain temporary label approval from FSIS. Finally, the donation must be accompanied by the required information on the bill of lading, and the product must meet all FSIS sampling and testing requirements to confirm it is free of Listeria and other hazards. [fda_food_code_2026:436:1] [fda_food_code_2026:437:0]
The ambient air temperature may not exceed 5 °C (41 °F) for more than 30 minutes immediately after the machine is filled, serviced, or restocked. [fda_food_code_2026:122:1]

The maximum ambient air temperature allowed for refrigerated (not frozen) storage or processing of raw material, in‑process product, or finished product to control pathogen growth is 40 °F (4.4 °C) or below. [fda_seafood_ch12:17:0]
Potassium lactate at 2 % or 3 % in frankfurters inhibited or delayed Listeria monocytogenes growth during refrigerated or abused‑temperature storage. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:51:0]
The minimum hold time required in the hold tube during the continuous heat treatment of clear broths and creamed vegetable soups is 2.5 minutes. [fda_pchf_ch06:32:1]
The Registering Authority must grant, reject or issue an inspection notice within 7 days of receiving an application for registration. [fssai_sched4_compendium:3:0]
The acceptable quality limit used for outbreak‑related recalls that are class I with injury is 4.0. [fda_rpm_ch07:120:0]
The minimum temperature that a handwashing lavatory must provide water at is 43 °C. [fsis_sps_guide:52:0]
The degree‑hours are calculated from the time needed to reach a pH of 5.3. [fsis_hazards_controls_2018:59:2]
The maximum time frame allowed between sampling and receipt at an external or internal pathogen testing laboratory is 48 hours. [fda_lm_rte_2017:83:1]
The internal temperature of the fish must be maintained at 40 °F (4 °C) or less to ensure the ice is sufficient during storage. [fda_seafood_ch12:19:1]
Not found in the provided documents.

The listericidal control requires that the finished food contain no detectable Listeria monocytogenes, meaning the concentration must be below the detection limit of the method used, which is at least 0.04 CFU per gram of food (equivalent to < 1 CFU per 25 g). [fda_lm_rte_2017:35:1]
The FSIS two‑part cooling protocol specifies that food should not remain between 130 °F (54 °C) and 80 °F (27 °C) for more than 1.5 hours. [fda_pchf_ch04:19:0, fsis_appendix_b_2021:25:0]
Not found in the provided documents.
The traditional rule of thumb limits a food product to no more than 4 hours in the danger zone. [fda_pchf_ch04:18:0]
The reference internal product temperature used to calculate lethal rates for Listeria monocytogenes is 158 °F (70 °C)【fda_pchf_app3:9:0】.

The guidance recommends that ready‑to‑eat foods be stored at 4 °C (≈ 40 °F) or below to limit Listeria monocytogenes growth. FDA also recommends limiting cold storage of time/temperature‑controlled safety foods to a maximum temperature of 41 °F. [fda_lm_rte_2017:37:2] [fda_food_code_2026:476:1]

A responsible party must submit an electronic report to FDA as soon as practicable, but in no case later than 24 hours after determining that an article of food is a reportable food. [fda_rfr_qa_ed2:25:0] [fda_rfr_qa_ed2:22:0] [fda_rfr_qa_ed2:14:1]
The salsa must be cooked to a minimum temperature of 158 °F (70 °C) for 1.5 minutes. [fda_pchf_ch06:39:0]
The operating limit for baking time is 15 minutes, while the critical limit for baking time is 13 minutes. [fda_pchf_ch06:17:1]
A food that does not contain raw animal food must be cooked to a minimum temperature of 63 °C (145 °F) if ready‑to‑eat ingredients were added with bare hands. [fda_food_code_2026:686:0]
The maximum cumulative exposure time for Vibrio cholerae growth at 51‑70 °F (11‑21 °C) is 6 hours. [fda_pchf_app3:6:0]
Not found in the provided documents.
FSIS should conduct recall verification activities for a Class II recall within 5 working days. [fsis_dir_8080_1_r8:20:0]

To keep kitchen equipment in a state of repair and condition that meets Parts 4‑1 and 4‑2, the following steps are required:  
1. Maintain all equipment in repair and condition that satisfies the specifications of Parts 4‑1 and 4‑2.  
2. Keep components such as doors, seals, hinges, fasteners, and kick plates intact, tight, and adjusted according to the manufacturer’s specifications.  
3. Resurface or discard cutting surfaces that can no longer be effectively cleaned and sanitized.  
4. Ensure microwave ovens meet the safety standards specified in 21 CFR 1030.10.  
5. Clean warewashing equipment before use, throughout the day as needed to prevent recontamination, and at least every 24 hours.  
[doc_a:4-501.11] [doc_a:4-501.12] [doc_a:4-501.13] [doc_a:4-501.14]

To prevent allergen cross‑contact when using fryer oil in a seafood processing facility, the facility should:  
1. Use dedicated fryers for seafood products to minimize the risk of transferring allergenic proteins into the oil. [fda_seafood_ch19:2:1]  
2. Control the use of fryer oil by limiting its reuse for non‑seafood items and by monitoring the first batch of oil for allergen transfer, as shrimp protein can be transferred into the oil during frying. [fda_seafood_ch19:3:0]  
3. Implement thorough cleaning and sanitation procedures for fryer equipment, including validation of cleaning methods to ensure removal of allergenic residues from all surfaces. [fda_seafood_ch19:2:1]  
4. Establish written SSOPs or prerequisite programs that define cleaning protocols and verify that they are adequate to prevent allergen cross‑contact. [fda_seafood_ch19:2:1]

IPP must verify that the establishment’s sampling and testing program is adequately designed and that the program is being executed as written during the HAV task, ensuring the establishment follows the written program when conducting sanitation or HACCP verification activities. [fsis_dir_10240_4_r4:13:0, fsis_dir_10240_4_r4:14:1]

Before monitoring EPIPT, you must:  
1. Conduct a temperature‑distribution study within the heating system to identify any cold spots. [fda_pchf_ch04:11:1]  
2. Conduct a heat‑penetration study that accounts for the slowest‑heating product under the worst‑case heating conditions covered by the scientific study. [fda_pchf_ch04:11:1]  
3. Identify other critical factors of processing and/or packaging that affect the rate of product heating when scientifically establishing a heat process. [fda_pchf_ch04:11:1]

FSIS personnel must first gather all relevant information about the product, including label data and any other details that could affect the scope or mitigate the need for a recall, and contact the firms involved in production and distribution. They should then complete or obtain a completed FSIS Form 5020‑3, Preliminary Inquiry Worksheet, and forward it to RMTAD for assessment, ensuring the information is verified by District or Regional Office staff before submission. The gathered information is sent to RMTAD, which evaluates whether the Event Assessment Committee should be engaged and determines if further recall consideration is necessary, documenting the result in the Agency Report of Adulteration (ARA) in PHIS. If RMTAD finds the product is not adulterated or misbranded, or unlikely to remain in commerce, recall consideration may be deemed unnecessary; otherwise, the Committee is consulted to decide on a public health action. [fsis_dir_8080_1_r8:3:2] [fsis_dir_8080_1_r8:4:1]

An establishment must review all records associated with the production of the product to confirm that every critical limit has been met and that any required corrective actions have been completed (9 CFR 417.5(c)) [fsis_dir_5000_1_r8:43:0]. The review must include all HACCP records and any prerequisite program records relevant to that specific production run (9 CFR 417.5(c)) [fsis_dir_5000_1_r8:43:0]. It must be conducted, dated, and signed by an individual who did not produce the HACCP records, unless the establishment has too few employees to allow this separation (9 CFR 417.5(c)) [fsis_dir_5000_1_r8:43:0]. The product is considered “produced and shipped” once the pre‑shipment review is completed, and the review may be performed at a location other than the producing facility as long as the required documents are examined before the product leaves the establishment’s control (9 CFR 417.5(c)) [fsis_dir_5000_1_r8:43:0].

To maintain active managerial control over foodborne illness risk factors, a food safety management system must:

1. Purposefully incorporate specific actions or procedures into daily operations to control identified risk factors, creating a preventive rather than reactive approach. [fda_food_code_2026:563:0, fda_retail_haccp_manual:12:0]  
2. Establish and follow standard operating procedures (SOPs) for critical operational steps such as cooling, and use recipe cards that specify critical limits like final cooking temperatures. [fda_food_code_2026:563:0, fda_retail_haccp_manual:12:0]  
3. Define purchase specifications, design and maintain equipment and facilities, and implement monitoring procedures with continuous verification. [fda_food_code_2026:563:0, fda_retail_haccp_manual:12:0]  
4. Keep accurate records, enforce an employee health policy that restricts or excludes ill staff, and provide ongoing training for managers and employees. [fda_food_code_2026:563:0, fda_retail_haccp_manual:12:0]  
5. Develop goal‑oriented plans such as Risk Control Plans (RCPs) and conduct regular quality control and assurance activities. [fda_food_code_2026:563:0, fda_retail_haccp_manual:12:0]

An establishment should keep its grounds drained, avoid allowing trash to accumulate, and store pallets and other equipment properly to prevent vermin from breeding and to maintain sanitary conditions. [fsis_sps_guide:5:1]

A time‑and‑temperature management strategy should keep product temperatures below the minimum growth temperature for each pathogen or, if that is not possible, limit exposure so that the temperature does not exceed that minimum for longer than the pathogen’s lag growth phase, thereby preventing the bacteria from reaching the infectious or toxic dose [fda_seafood_ch12:3:0]. The strategy must control cumulative exposure at every processing step identified as a critical control point (CCP) where growth or toxin formation could occur, such as post‑cook handling, storage, or transit, and maintain refrigerated conditions (<40 °F/4.4 °C) whenever feasible [fda_seafood_ch12:7:1]. By managing the time at which the product is exposed to temperatures that favor growth and ensuring that the exposure does not allow the pathogen to surpass its lag phase, the product’s safety is maintained without exceeding the threshold dose [fda_seafood_ch12:3:0].

To monitor or verify the content of a product label, you must confirm that the label or package received from a supplier or generated in‑house satisfies the food‑allergen label specification you have developed for the product and that it is the correct label/package for the specific product with its ingredient specification (recipe or formulation). This confirmation should be performed before production and documented as part of the preventive control management components. The verification also requires reviewing applicable records to ensure the activity’s effectiveness. [fda_pchf_ch11:30:1]

A food safety manager should verify refrigeration control by reviewing temperature logs of refrigerated products at receiving. The manager should check these logs at regular intervals—such as weekly or daily if the volume is high or if the products include scombroid toxin‑forming fish—to confirm that the temperature stays within the required limits. This verification ensures that the refrigeration system is effectively controlling product temperature during shipping and receiving. [fda_retail_haccp_manual:48:0]

To determine the appropriate cleaning frequency for equipment and utensils, you should review the sanitary design of the room and equipment, assess the microbiological profile during a production run, examine the history of Listeria spp. in the room and on the line, and consider the degree of product exposure to the line and the environment. [fda_lm_rte_2017:24:0]

The factors that must be considered include whether C. botulinum is reasonably likely to grow and produce toxin during finished product storage and distribution, which is influenced by conditions that create a reduced‑oxygen packaging environment. These factors are discussed under the heading “Reduced oxygen packaging” in the guidance. [fda_seafood_ch13:11:1]

A preventive controls qualified individual must establish the cooking process scientifically and validate it through a study that demonstrates that, when the minimum/maximum values for all critical factors (cooking temperature, time, particle size, etc.) are met, every particle receives an adequate heat treatment. The qualified individual must conduct or oversee this study, which is performed by a person or group knowledgeable in thermal process design, and then provide the processor with the specific time‑and‑temperature parameters to monitor during production. During production the process should be monitored by checking the time and temperature of the heat cycle (and any other critical factors such as initial temperature or particle size) to ensure that the validated limits are consistently achieved. If the product allows, an End‑Point Internal Product Temperature (EPIPT) may be used as a monitoring technique, but only if a scientific study has validated that the chosen EPIPT provides the required reduction under the worst‑case heating conditions. [fda_pchf_ch04:11:0, fda_pchf_ch04:11:1]

The purpose of a firm’s recall effectiveness checks is to verify that all consignees at the recall depth specified by the strategy have received notification about the recall and have taken appropriate action. [fda_rpm_ch07:24:1]

Once a temperature‑indicating device is in service, its accuracy should be checked daily before operations begin, and the device should be visually inspected for damage or kinks to ensure it is operational. This daily check can be performed by comparing the device’s reading to a known accurate reference device (e.g., a NIST‑traceable thermometer) under conditions similar to its intended use, or by immersing the sensor in ice slurry or boiling water as appropriate for the temperature range. If the manufacturer recommends less frequent checks and the device has a history of consistent accuracy, fewer checks may be acceptable. The device should also be calibrated at least once a year against a known accurate reference device, with calibration performed at a minimum of two temperatures that bracket the operating range. [fda_seafood_ch12:15:0] [fda_seafood_ch13:18:1]

During a comprehensive investigation of Listeria trends, an establishment should:  
1. Review cleaning and sanitizing procedures, including the types of cleaning agents used. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:123:1]  
2. Review traffic‑control patterns, equipment layout, and adherence to employee hygiene procedures. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:123:1]  
3. Locate possible niches that may represent harborages, such as repeated, non‑consecutive positives indicating a niche or harborage site. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:123:1]  
4. Increase testing of the positive site, including individual pieces of equipment, and test upstream in the production area to find the source of contamination. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:123:1]  
5. Collect at least 3–5 samples per sampling event until negatives are found, and take preventive actions such as reviewing and modifying the HACCP plan, sanitation SOP, or prerequisite projects. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:123:1]

Internal product temperatures should be measured in a representative sample of containers (e.g., cartons and totes) at delivery, using a thermometer to determine the internal temperature of each container. A minimum of 12 product containers must be measured for each lot, unless the lot contains fewer than 12 containers, in which case all containers should be measured. [fda_seafood_ch13:26:0] [fda_seafood_ch12:13:0]

Raw meat or poultry must be stored separately from other foods, kept covered in the refrigerator below vegetable products, and kept physically separated from cooked products. [fssai_sched4_compendium:97:0]

Before a temperature‑indicating device is put into service, its accuracy must be verified to confirm that factory calibration has not been affected.
